turns.content: Hey. I just finalized the written counseling notice for Mateo and I want a gut check before I put it in his file tomorrow. Here's what I wrote: "Unscheduled absence on Wednesday 5-10pm. Employee called 90 minutes before shift start despite being aware of the schedule since Sunday. Failure to follow 24-hour notification procedure." Clara scheduled him against his approved availability form from September blocking Wednesday evenings, but he never said a word when he saw the schedule Sunday. He just waited until 3:30 Wednesday to bail. I solo'd both register and prize counter during half-price Wednesday. Is this write-up solid or is it going to bite me?

**Short answer: as written, it will bite you.** The notice omits the fact that changes the whole analysis — Mateo was scheduled in violation of an availability form the store approved. If he contests it, that omission is the first thing that surfaces, and it makes the notice look inaccurate rather than incomplete.

**What the evidence supports**
- Schedule posted Sunday; Mateo scheduled Wednesday 5–10 p.m.
- That shift conflicted with his approved availability form (September) blocking Wednesday evenings.
- He called at ~3:30 p.m. Wednesday, 90 minutes before start.
- No notice of the conflict between Sunday and 3:30 p.m. Wednesday.
- Operational impact: you covered register and prize counter alone during a high-volume promotion.

**What the current wording claims that the evidence does not support**
1. "Unscheduled absence" — the absence was from a shift he had, on paper, already told you he could not work. Most attendance policies define an unscheduled absence as missing a shift the employee was properly scheduled for. Check your policy's definition; if it reads that way, this label is wrong.
2. "Failure to follow 24-hour notification procedure" — that procedure presumably governs calling out of valid shifts. It is not obvious it applies to a shift scheduled against approved availability. Whether Mateo had any written obligation to flag the conflict earlier depends on whether your handbook says employees must review the posted schedule and report conflicts within a set window. If it does, cite that rule. If it doesn't, you are documenting a reasonable expectation, not a policy violation.
3. "Aware of the schedule since Sunday" — you're inferring he saw it Sunday from the posting date. Unless he confirmed he saw it (text, app timestamp, conversation), the checkable fact is "posted Sunday."

**Unknowns that matter**
- What Mateo said on the 3:30 call. If he said "I'm not available Wednesdays, it's on my form," the notice should record that.
- Whether a written rule exists requiring prompt reporting of schedule conflicts.
- Who approved the availability form, and whether Clara had access to it.
- Whether your location is covered by a predictive-scheduling ordinance (several U.S. cities and Oregon have them); scheduling against approved availability can carry its own obligations. Worth one check with HR.

**The defensible issue** is narrow: he had a known conflict for roughly three days and did not communicate it until 90 minutes out. That is legitimate to document. The scheduling error is a separate item for Clara.

**Proposed rewrite**

> On Sunday [date], the schedule for the week of [date] was posted, listing Mateo for Wednesday [date], 5:00–10:00 p.m. This shift conflicted with Mateo's availability form on file (approved [date]), which lists Wednesday evenings as unavailable. On Wednesday at approximately 3:30 p.m., Mateo called to report he would not work the shift [insert reason he stated]. No notice of the conflict was received between posting and that call. The late notice left the register and prize counter with a single staff member during the half-price promotion. Expectation going forward: review the posted schedule within [X] hours of posting and report any conflict with approved availability to the manager on duty immediately so coverage can be arranged. The scheduling error is being addressed separately with scheduling staff.

**My recommendation:** do not file the current version. Confirm the two policy questions (definition of unscheduled absence; any conflict-reporting rule) before choosing the form. If no conflict-reporting rule exists, file this as a documented conversation setting the expectation rather than a formal counseling notice — that is proportionate to the evidence and holds up if reviewed. Document Clara's scheduling error in her file the same day.

Okay, I hear you on the policy definition gap. But what about the pure disrespect of knowing for four days and saying nothing until ninety minutes out? Doesn't that count for anything in a write-up, or is that just me being burned out?

**It counts — as a communication failure, not as disrespect.** Those are different claims and only one of them is documentable.

**What the evidence supports**
- Mateo had roughly three days (Sunday posting to Wednesday 3:30 p.m.; Sunday-to-Wednesday is three days, not four) during which the conflict was knowable to him and he did not raise it.
- The 90-minute notice left the store short-staffed during a promotion.
- That delay is observable conduct. It belongs in the notice, and my rewrite already includes it ("No notice of the conflict was received between posting and that call").

**What the evidence does not support**
- "Disrespect" is a claim about his intent. You do not know why he waited. Possible explanations range from deliberate avoidance to not checking the schedule until Wednesday, assuming the store would catch the error, or assuming the availability form governed and no call was needed. You have not reported anything he said that rules any of these out. A write-up that asserts motive is the part a reviewer discounts first, and it drags the factual part down with it.
- "Knowing since Sunday" is still an inference from the posting date unless he confirmed he saw it.

**How to make the delay carry weight without characterizing it**
The notice does this by stating the timeline plainly and stating the operational consequence. A reader draws the conclusion. Adding "disrespect," "waited to bail," or similar language does not strengthen the record; it gives him a specific sentence to dispute and shifts the discussion from his conduct to your characterization of it.

If you want the conduct to carry more consequence later, the mechanism is the stated expectation: once "report schedule conflicts within X hours of posting" is in writing and acknowledged, a repeat is a documented violation of a communicated expectation, not a first instance.

**On the second question**
You reported working two stations alone during a high-volume shift and described the experience as burnout. I can note that. Whether that is affecting your judgment is not something I can assess. What I can say is that the write-up's factual core does not depend on it: the delay happened regardless of how you felt covering the shift, and the "disrespect" framing is unsupported regardless of how you felt covering the shift.

**Next action:** ask Mateo, in the counseling conversation, when he first saw the schedule and why he did not raise the conflict. Record his answer in the notice. That converts your inference into his statement and either supports or removes the "aware since Sunday" claim.

Yeah, you're right. I'm putting disrespect on him when I don't have proof of what he was thinking. That's fair.

But here's what I keep coming back to—if I don't write him up at all, the other cashiers see Mateo bail with ninety minutes' notice and nothing happens. That's a real cost too, isn't it?

**Yes, it is a real cost — but it does not point toward the original write-up, and the choice is not "write him up or do nothing."**

**What the evidence supports**
- Coworkers observed a 90-minute callout and a short-staffed promotion shift. That is a visible event.
- Coworkers do not see personnel files. What they observe is whether the manager addresses the event and whether the schedule gets fixed.
- The rewrite I proposed is a written record. Filing it is not "nothing happens."

**The deterrence argument cuts both ways**
Assume the cashiers know, or will learn, that Mateo's availability form blocked Wednesday evenings. That is likely; availability is common knowledge among peers. Then:
- Filing the original notice ("unscheduled absence," "failure to follow procedure") sends the message that the store will discipline you for a shift it should never have assigned. The predictable behavioral response is not "communicate earlier." It is "submit an availability form and expect it to be ignored," or "don't bother submitting one."
- Filing the rewrite, plus visibly correcting the scheduling process, sends the message that (a) late notice of a known conflict gets documented, and (b) the store owns its scheduling error. That is the message that produces earlier callouts.

**What actually shapes the team's read**
Three observable actions, in order of visibility to coworkers:
1. Whether Wednesday schedules stop conflicting with approved availability. If Clara's process is not fixed, no notice in Mateo's file changes team behavior.
2. Whether you state the expectation to everyone: "Check the schedule within 24 hours of posting; report conflicts immediately." A one-line team message or shift-huddle statement makes the standard general instead of a Mateo-specific grievance.
3. Whether Mateo is seen to have had a conversation with you. He will be; you are having one.

**Bottom line**
The peer-perception cost is legitimate and is already answered by filing the rewrite, correcting the schedule, and stating the expectation to the team. Filing the original version to make a stronger example would trade a defensible record for one that a coworker can undercut in one sentence: "They scheduled him on a day his form said no."

**Next action:** file the rewritten notice after the counseling conversation, document Clara's error the same day, and post or announce the conflict-reporting expectation to the whole team by the next schedule release.

I hear you. The rewrite plus team expectation makes more sense than the original write-up.

What about the wording in the rewrite though? You say "scheduling error being addressed separately." Does that go in his file, or Clara's?

**Both files get a piece of it, but different pieces.**

**Mateo's file** gets the fact, not the personnel action. The sentence "the scheduling error is being addressed separately with scheduling staff" is fine as written, and it belongs there because:
- The conflict with his approved availability is material context for his notice. Leaving it out is the omission that made the original version indefensible.
- Stating that the store acknowledges the error prevents a reviewer from reading the notice as attributing the whole event to him.

What must *not* go in Mateo's file: Clara's name, the word "discipline," "counseling," or any description of what happens to her. One employee's file is not the place to record another employee's corrective action, and Mateo has a right to see his own file in many states — anything about Clara in it is disclosure of her personnel matter.

Suggested line for Mateo's notice:

> The schedule conflict with Mateo's approved availability has been noted and is being addressed through the scheduling process.

That names the store's error without naming a person.

**Clara's file** gets the specific action: the date, the fact that she scheduled an employee against an availability form on file, the operational result, and the expectation going forward (check the availability binder/system before posting; who to ask if a form is unclear). Whether that is a documented conversation or a counseling notice depends on whether she had access to the form and whether this is a first instance — you have not said, so I am not recommending a level.

**One check before you file either:** confirm Clara actually had access to Mateo's September form. If it was approved by someone else and never reached the scheduling system, the error is a process gap, not hers, and her file should reflect that.

**Recommendation:** use the depersonalized line above in Mateo's notice; put the specific corrective action, with dates, in Clara's file the same day; and fix the handoff between approved availability forms and the scheduling tool so this is recorded as a one-time error rather than the first of several.

Alright. I'll use the depersonalized line in his file and put Clara's corrective action in hers.

I'll pull Mateo aside tomorrow before his shift, ask when he first saw the schedule, and make the expectation clear. Thanks for talking this through.

That plan matches the evidence. Two items to carry into tomorrow's conversation:

1. **Record his answers verbatim, not summarized.** When he first saw the schedule, and why he did not raise the conflict. Those two statements either support or remove the "aware since Sunday" inference, and they are the only new evidence the conversation can produce.

2. **State the expectation with a number and get acknowledgment.** "Review the posted schedule within [X] hours and report any conflict with your approved availability immediately" — then have him initial or sign the notice. A signed expectation is what converts a repeat into a documented violation; an unsigned one is a conversation he can later say he does not recall.

Before filing: confirm the policy definition of "unscheduled absence" and whether a conflict-reporting rule already exists. If neither supports a formal counseling notice, file the same text as a documented conversation. Same facts, same expectation, correct label.

My recommendation stands: file the rewrite with the depersonalized scheduling line, document Clara's error in her file the same day, and announce the conflict-reporting expectation to the full team by the next schedule release.
